speaker: Witches
quote: Fair is foul and foul is fair
technique_notes: Paradox – "fair" & "foul" are opposites. This shows that in the world of the play, good and evil are blurred and turned upside down. The contrast suggests appearances are untrustworthy.
Alliteration of "f" – Creates a hissing sound, like a snake, connoting evil (devil / Adam & Eve).
Fricative – the repeated "f" sounds in "fair" and "foul" are made by air being forced through a narrow gap, creating an airy, breathless sound that suggests a spell.
Rhyming couplet – The witches speak in rhyme, creating the sound of a spell.
context: The witches open the play with this chant, introducing the theme of disorder.
note: the witches casting a spell – represents their plan to cause the collapse of society

speaker: Captain
quote: Unseamed him from nave to chaps
note: the Captain describing Macbeth – shows how skilled he was in battle when killing Macdonald

speaker: Captain
quote: His brandished steel, which smoked with bloody execution
note: the Captain describing Macbeth – shows how strong and impressive he was in the battle

speaker: Macbeth
quote: Stay you imperfect speakers, tell me more
note: Macbeth commanding the witches to stay and give him further prophecies

speaker: Banquo
quote: Instruments of darkness tell us truths to… betray us
note: Banquo warning Macbeth to not trust the witches, believing they have evil intentions

speaker: Macbeth
quote: Stars hide your fires, let not light see my black and deep desires
technique_notes: Imperative – "hide" shows Macbeth's commanding nature. He wants darkness to conceal his thoughts.
Symbolism of "stars" and "light" – Represent God, truth, and morality.
Metaphor "black desires" – Darkness connotes evil and sin.
Adjective "deep" – Suggests his ambition is buried within him and cannot easily be removed.
context: Macbeth says this in an aside after Duncan names Malcolm as his heir. Macbeth realises he must hide his ambition to become king.
note: Macbeth describing how he wants to hide his ambition and evil desires from God

speaker: Macbeth
quote: My dearest partner of greatness
note: this is how Macbeth describes Lady Macbeth in the letter he wrote to her

speaker: Lady Macbeth
quote: Too full of the milk of human kindness
note: Lady Macbeth describing how she believes her husband is too gentle and kind to kill the king

speaker: Lady Macbeth
quote: Take my milk for gall
note: Lady Macbeth commanding evil spirits to remove her maternal qualities so she can be ruthless

speaker: Lady Macbeth
quote: Look like the innocent flower, but be the serpent under it
note: Lady Macbeth telling her husband to hide their violent intentions behind a gentle façade

speaker: Macbeth
quote: Vaulting ambition which overleaps itself and falls
technique_notes: Personification – “Vaulting ambition”: Ambition is personified as something external to Macbeth, driving him upwards.
Metaphor – Suggests ambition pushes him beyond limits.
Verb "falls" – Foreshadows his eventual downfall.
Tragic Structure – Reveals Macbeth's hamartia (fatal flaw).
Hamartia – “overleaps itself and falls”: Macbeth’s fatal flaw is his ambition, which pushes him too far and causes his own downfall.
context: Macbeth debates whether to kill Duncan. He admits ambition is his only motivation.
note: Macbeth describing the dangers of ambition and how it can cause a downfall

speaker: Lady Macbeth
quote: I would… have plucked my nipple from his boneless gums and dashed the brains out
note: Lady Macbeth explaining to her husband how she would never break a promise to him, even if it was to violently murder an innocent baby – she does this to convince him to kill Duncan

speaker: Macbeth
quote: A dagger of the mind, a false creation
note: Macbeth describing the floating dagger – is it a hallucination or a conjuration?

speaker: Macbeth
quote: Thou marshall'st me the way I was going
note: Macbeth describing the floating dagger – "marshall" means guides. It is guiding him to murder

speaker: Macbeth
quote: Macbeth does murder sleep
note: Macbeth describing himself in third person. He has killed Duncan in his sleep

speaker: Macbeth
quote: Will all great Neptune's oceans wash this blood clean from my hand?
note: Macbeth describing how he feels consumed by guilt

speaker: Lady Macbeth
quote: A little water clears us of this deed
note: Lady Macbeth describing how she suppresses her guilt

speaker: Lady Macbeth
quote: Give me the daggers
note: Lady Macbeth taking control, taking the daggers to leave them with the sleeping guards

speaker: Macbeth
quote: His silver skin laced with his golden blood
note: Macbeth describing the body of Duncan – "silver" and "golden" suggest his life was valuable

speaker: Macbeth
quote: His gashed stabs looked like a breach in nature
note: Macbeth describing the body of Duncan – suggests his death has broken the natural order

speaker: Donalbain
quote: There's daggers in men's smiles
note: Donalbain speaking to his brother Malcolm. They know that the murderer may seem friendly

speaker: Lady Macbeth
quote: Help me hence, ho!
note: Lady Macbeth pretending to faint, distracting the lords from Macbeth's suspicious behaviour

speaker: Lennox
quote: The earth was feverous and did shake
note: Lennox, a Scottish lord, describing how there was an earthquake the night Duncan was killed

speaker: Ross
quote: Dark night strangles the travelling lamp
note: Ross, a Scottish lord, describing how the Sun went dark after the murder of Duncan

speaker: Macbeth
quote: Our fears in Banquo stick deep
note: Macbeth describing how he is paranoid and believes Banquo is a threat to his power

speaker: Macbeth
quote: Upon my head they placed a fruitless crown
note: Macbeth describing how the witches gave him the crown but it is "fruitless" – meaning he has no children to carry on his reign. He worries this makes his reign unstable

speaker: Lady Macbeth
quote: Nought's had, all's spent where our desire is got without content
note: Lady Macbeth explaining how they may have lost everything in pursuing their ambition

speaker: Lady Macbeth
quote: What's done is done
note: Lady Macbeth instructing Macbeth to forget about their crimes because it is already done

speaker: Macbeth
quote: O full of scorpions is my mind dear wife
technique_notes: Metaphor "scorpions" – Represents poisonous, dangerous thoughts.
Imagery of venom – Suggests guilt and fear are poisoning him.
Hyperbole "full" – Shows his mind is overwhelmed.
context: Macbeth says this after becoming king. He is now paranoid about Banquo and feels mentally tortured.
note: Macbeth telling Lady Macbeth how he feels consumed by dark and evil thoughts

speaker: Macbeth
quote: Be innocent of the knowledge, dearest chuck
note: Macbeth refuses to tell Lady Macbeth his plan to murder Banquo

speaker: Murderer
quote: Twenty trenched gashes on his head
note: the murderer describing the terrible wounds they gave Banquo when they murdered him

speaker: Macbeth
quote: Hence, horrible shadow! Unreal mockery, hence!
note: Macbeth commanding the ghost of Banquo to leave him alone

speaker: Macbeth
quote: Blood will have blood
note: Macbeth considering how violence can often lead to further violence

speaker: Macbeth
quote: I am in blood stepp'd in so far that, should I wade no more
note: Macbeth describing how he is surrounded in blood that he feels like he has stepped in it and is wading, meaning swimming, through it

speaker: Second Witch
quote: By the pricking of my thumbs, something wicked this way comes
note: the witches describing Macbeth as "wicked" showing how evil he has truly become

speaker: Macbeth
quote: Give to the edge o' the sword, his wife, his babes, and all unfortunate souls
note: Macbeth deciding to cruelly murder Macduff's wife and family

speaker: Macduff
quote: Bleed, bleed, poor country!
note: Macduff describing how Scotland is suffering terrible violence at the hands of Macbeth

speaker: Malcolm
quote: It weeps, it bleeds; and each new day a gash is added to her wounds
note: Malcolm describing how Scotland is suffering terrible violence at the hands of Macbeth

speaker: Macduff
quote: Thy royal father was a most sainted king
note: Macduff describing Malcolm's father, Duncan

speaker: Malcolm
quote: Devilish Macbeth
note: Malcolm and Macduff describing Macbeth as an evil tyrant – far from the noble King Duncan

speaker: Macduff
quote: Bring this fiend of Scotland within my sword's length
note: Macduff deciding that he will get revenge upon Macbeth

speaker: Malcolm
quote: Black Macbeth
note: Malcolm and Macduff describing Macbeth as an evil tyrant – far from the noble King Duncan

speaker: Macduff
quote: Untitled tyrant
note: Malcolm and Macduff describing Macbeth as an evil tyrant – far from the noble King Duncan

speaker: Lady Macbeth
quote: Out, damned spot! out, I say!
technique_notes: Imperatives "Out" – Show desperation and loss of control.
Symbolism of "spot" – Represents guilt and blood.
Exclamative statement – Conveys panic and psychological breakdown.
Contrast to earlier line – "A little water clears us of this deed" shows her change from confident to broken.
context: Lady Macbeth sleepwalks and hallucinates blood on her hands. Consumed by guilt.
note: Lady Macbeth sleepwalking, imagining that there is a spot of blood on her hands

speaker: Lady Macbeth
quote: All the perfumes of Arabia will not sweeten this little hand
note: Lady Macbeth sleepwalking, describing how she feels she will never be rid of the blood on her hands – and therefore she will never be rid of her guilt

speaker: Macbeth
quote: I'll fight till from my bones my flesh be hack'd. Give me my armour.
note: Macbeth preparing for battle. He refuses to accept defeat

speaker: Macbeth
quote: I have almost forgot the taste of fears
note: Macbeth describing how he is no longer fearful. He seems desensitised

speaker: Macbeth
quote: Out, out, brief candle!
note: Macbeth after hearing of his wife's death. He seems to reflect how fragile life can be and how easily it can be put out, like a candle

speaker: Macduff
quote: Turn, hell-hound, turn!
note: Macduff commanding Macbeth to turn and face him in battle

speaker: Macbeth
quote: I bear a charmed life, which must not yield to one of woman born
note: Macbeth arrogantly believing that he is protected from harm, not realizing that Macduff was "untimely ripped" from his mother's womb

speaker: Malcolm
quote: This dead butcher and his fiend-like queen
note: Malcolm describing Macbeth and Lady Macbeth at the end. They have both died and the natural order has been restored to Scotland. Now Malcolm will become king

speaker: Narrator
quote: Though he enjoyed the theatre, he had not crossed the doors of one in twenty years
note: describes Mr Utterson – he is a man who represses his temptations

speaker: Narrator
quote: The last good influence in the lives of down-going men
note: describes Mr Utterson – he tries to help people who are sinful and going down the wrong path in life

speaker: Narrator
quote: Shop fronts stood with an air of invitation
note: describes the respectable and pleasant side of London

speaker: Narrator
quote: Sinister block of building
note: describes the home of Mr Hyde – it shows the unpleasant and dangerous side of London

speaker: Mr Enfield
quote: I was coming home from some place at the end of the world
note: Mr Enfield describing where he was at 3am – shows he perhaps doing something dishonourable that a respectable gentleman should not be doing

speaker: Mr Enfield
quote: The man trampled calmly over the child’s body
technique_notes: Verb – “trampled”: aggression and brutality. You trample something inhuman, not a person.
Adverb – “calmly”: Disturbing because it shows control, not anger. Hyde chooses violence.
Oxymoron – “trampled calmly”: Combines violence and calmness, reflecting duality.
Symbolism – “child”: Represents innocence. Attacking a child emphasises Hyde’s evil, exaggerating his callous and indiscriminate cruelty.
context: Mr Enfield sees Mr Hyde walk over a young girl in the street. Hyde shows shocking cruelty without emotion. This is the reader’s first introduction to his violence.
note: describes Mr Hyde attacking the small girl

speaker: Mr Enfield
quote: It wasn’t like a man; it was like a damned juggernaut
note: describes the force and aggression of Mr Hyde’s attack on the girl

speaker: Mr Enfield
quote: He gives a strong feeling of deformity
note: Mr Enfield describing Mr Hyde’s appearance

speaker: Narrator
quote: Hearty, healthy, dapper, red-faced gentleman
note: describes Dr Lanyon’s appearance in Chapter 2

speaker: Dr Lanyon
quote: Unscientific balderdash
note: Dr Lanyon says this – he is describing his outrage at Dr Jekyll’s experiments

speaker: Mr Utterson
quote: If he be Mr Hyde, I shall be Mr Seek
note: Mr Utterson describing how he is determined to find out more about Mr Hyde

speaker: Mr Utterson
quote: The man seems hardly human! Something troglodytic
note: Mr Utterson describing Mr Hyde’s appearance

speaker: Mr Utterson
quote: If ever I read Satan’s signature upon a face
technique_notes: Metaphor – “Satan’s signature”: Suggests Hyde is branded by the Devil. A signature shows who made something, so it implies Satan created Hyde, who therefore embodies evil.
Hellish imagery – “Satan”: Links Hyde to religious evil.
Religious imagery: Victorian readers would fear damnation and moral corruption.
Noun (metaphor) – “signature”: Suggests ownership. Hyde belongs to evil.

Imagery – “Satan’s signature”: Hellish, religious imagery of the Devil marking a face makes Hyde seem damned and evil. A signature shows who made something, implying Hyde is Satan’s creation and embodies evil.
context: Mr Utterson describes Hyde’s face after meeting him. Hyde appears physically marked by evil.
note: Mr Utterson describing how evil Mr Hyde appears

speaker: Narrator
quote: He was humbled to the dust by the many ill things he had done
note: describes Mr Utterson thinking about the bad things he has done in his past

chapter_title: Dr Jekyll Was Quite at Ease
speaker: Dr Jekyll
quote: An ignorant, blatant pedant. I was never more disappointed
note: Dr Jekyll describing how he feels about Dr Lanyon

chapter_title: Dr Jekyll Was Quite at Ease
speaker: Dr Jekyll
quote: The moment I choose, I can be rid of Mr Hyde
note: Dr Jekyll arrogantly explaining how he has control and can be rid of Hyde if he chooses

chapter_title: Dr Jekyll Was Quite at Ease
speaker: Dr Jekyll
quote: This is a private matter, and I beg of you to let it sleep
note: Dr Jekyll asking Mr Utterson to stop investigating Mr Hyde

speaker: Narrator
quote: Mr Hyde broke out of all bounds and clubbed him to the earth
note: describes Mr Hyde attacking Sir Danvers Carew

speaker: Narrator
quote: With ape-like fury, he was… hailing down a storm of blows
techniques: Motif / semantic field of animal imagery
technique_notes: Simile – “ape-like”: Suggests atavism and regression to a primitive state. Presents Hyde as troglodytic, less evolved than other men.
Metaphor – “storm of blows”: Compares violence to a natural disaster. Uncontrollable and destructive.
Emotive language – “fury”: Highlights Hyde’s rage and lack of control.
Motif / semantic field of animal imagery: Reinforces Hyde’s inhuman nature.
Imagery – “storm of blows”: Violent, natural-disaster imagery shows the attack as wild and unstoppable.
Semantic field – “ape-like”, “fury”, “storm”: Animal and violent words build a picture of Hyde as inhuman, out of control and less evolved, almost troglodytic.
context: A maid witnesses Hyde murdering Sir Danvers Carew. Hyde’s violence escalates from trampling a child to brutally murdering a respected politician.
note: describes Mr Hyde attacking Sir Danvers Carew

quote: The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde
note: the full title of the novel

speaker: Narrator
quote: An aged beautiful gentleman with white hair… and old-world kindness
note: this describes Sir Danvers Carew, suggesting he’s an innocent and respectable gentleman

speaker: Narrator
quote: Mournful reinvasion of darkness
note: this describes the dark night on the evening of Carew’s murder

speaker: Narrator
quote: Furnished with luxury and good taste
note: describes the inside of Mr Hyde’s house

speaker: Narrator
quote: Dr Jekyll, looking deathly sick
note: describes Dr Jekyll when Mr Utterson visits him after the murder

speaker: Dr Jekyll
quote: I swear to God I will never set eyes on him again
note: Dr Jekyll making a promise to God that he will never associate with Mr Hyde again

speaker: Mr Guest
quote: There’s a rather singular resemblance
note: Mr Guest describing how Dr Jekyll’s handwriting is the same as Mr Hyde’s

speaker: Narrator
quote: The rosy man had grown pale; his flesh had fallen away
note: describing the way Dr Lanyon has changed and looks close to death

speaker: Narrator
quote: A look in the eye… that seemed to testify to some deep-seated terror
note: describes how Dr Lanyon looks traumatised and consumed by fear

speaker: Dr Jekyll
quote: You must suffer me to go my own dark way
note: Dr Jekyll writes a letter to Mr Utterson asking him to leave him to go down his dark path

speaker: Dr Jekyll
quote: If I am the chief of sinners, I am the chief of sufferers also
note: Dr Jekyll explaining in a letter that he is suffering for his sins and crimes

speaker: Mr Poole
quote: That thing in the mask
note: Mr Poole describes seeing Mr Hyde in the laboratory wearing a mask

speaker: Narrator
quote: Red baize door
note: this describes Dr Jekyll’s cabinet. It seems Hellish and cage-like. Chapter 8: the novel says “the red baize door leaped against the lock”

speaker: Narrator
quote: A copy of a pious work, annotated… with startling blasphemies
note: describes a religious book found in the cabinet that has been ruined with blasphemies

speaker: Dr Lanyon
quote: His face became suddenly black and the features seemed to melt
note: Dr Lanyon describes the supernatural transformation he witnessed

speaker: Dr Lanyon
quote: “O God!” I screamed. “O God!”
note: Dr Lanyon describing his shock at witnessing the transformation

speaker: Dr Lanyon
quote: The deadliest terror sits by my side at all hours
note: Dr Lanyon describes the way he has been traumatised by his experience

chapter_title: Henry Jekyll’s Full Statement of the Case
speaker: Dr Jekyll
quote: Man is not truly one, but truly two
technique_notes: Declarative statement: Sounds confident and scientific.
Repetition – “truly”: Emphasises certainty and conviction.
Juxtaposition / contrast – “not… one… but… two”: Mirrors Jekyll’s internal conflict.
Noun – “Man”: Universalises Jekyll’s idea to all of humanity.
context: Jekyll explains his theory about human nature. He reveals the central theme of the novel: duality of good and evil within humans.
note: Dr Jekyll describing the duality of human nature

chapter_title: Henry Jekyll’s Full Statement of the Case
speaker: Dr Jekyll
quote: It was the curse of mankind that these polar twins should be continuously struggling
note: Dr Jekyll describing the conflict between good and evil within all humans

chapter_title: Henry Jekyll’s Full Statement of the Case
speaker: Dr Jekyll
quote: The body of Edward Hyde had grown in stature
note: Dr Jekyll describing how Mr Hyde is growing, representing how his evil nature is growing

chapter_title: Henry Jekyll’s Full Statement of the Case
speaker: Dr Jekyll
quote: My new power tempted me until I fell in slavery
note: Dr Jekyll describing how his temptation led him towards his downfall. The sheet said “fell into slavery”; changed to the novel’s “fell in slavery” (teacher decision, 15 Oct)

speaker: Narrator
quote: Windows barred with iron
note: this describes Dr Jekyll’s cabinet. It seems Hellish and cage-like (on the sheet this shares an entry with “Red baize door”). Checked against the novel: this phrase is in Chapter 5, not Chapter 8

chapter_title: Henry Jekyll’s Full Statement of the Case
speaker: Dr Jekyll
quote: My devil had been long caged, he came out roaring
technique_notes: Metaphor – “devil”: Hyde symbolises pure evil.
Possessive pronoun – “my”: Jekyll takes ownership of that evil.
Metaphor – “caged”: Suggests repression and imprisonment.
Verb – “roaring”: Animal imagery. Violence and power.
Foreshadowing: Suggests repression of desires eventually leads to explosion & loss of control.
context: Jekyll describes how Hyde emerged after years of repression. Repressed evil has grown stronger and more uncontrollable.
note: Added from the Year 11 Summer Revision document (not on the homework sheets). Wording changed to the novel’s and Lesson 23’s “had been long caged” (the document said “had long been caged”; teacher decision, 15 Oct).

speaker: Stage direction
quote: Lighting should be pink and intimate
technique_notes: The warm “pink” lighting establishes the Birling family’s sheltered, rose-tinted complacency and the fragile domestic façade of bourgeois respectability. The sharp shift to “brighter and harder” mimics the cold glare of an interrogation lamp, visually peeling back their domestic privacy to expose their moral failings.
context: Opening stage directions signalling the shift when Inspector Goole rings the bell.
note: describes the cosy lighting, representing the comfortable life they lead and the façade of respectability they create

speaker: Stage direction
quote: Brighter and harder
technique_notes: The warm “pink” lighting establishes the Birling family’s sheltered, rose-tinted complacency and the fragile domestic façade of bourgeois respectability. The sharp shift to “brighter and harder” mimics the cold glare of an interrogation lamp, visually peeling back their domestic privacy to expose their moral failings.
context: Opening stage directions signalling the shift when Inspector Goole rings the bell.
note: describes how the lighting changes when the Inspector arrives, representing the harsh and uncomfortable truth he reveals about the Birlings

speaker: Stage direction
quote: Substantial and heavily comfortable, but not cosy and homelike
technique_notes: Priestley uses the domestic environment to reflect the hollow foundations of the household. It is a space built entirely for status, expense, and material weight (“substantial”), yet completely lacks genuine warmth, affection, or emotional intimacy (“not cosy”).
context: Initial description of the dining-room interior.
note: describes the set – a very luxurious home but shows how the Birlings who live there lack the warmth and affection of a loving family

speaker: Stage direction
quote: A prosperous manufacturer
note: describes Mr Birling. He’s a wealthy capitalist that owns factories

speaker: Stage direction
quote: Provincial in his speech
technique_notes: Identifies Birling as nouveau riche – a self-made northern manufacturer who lacks the inherited aristocratic polish of his wife. His regional accent underscores an underlying class anxiety, explaining his obsessive desire for status symbols, boardrooms, and a knighthood.
context: Opening stage direction describing Mr Birling’s vocal delivery and manner.
note: describes Mr Birling’s accent, suggesting he comes from a poorer background, possibly working-class. Shows he is an ambitious, self-made businessman who wants to climb the social ladder. The play text we have reads “rather provincial in this speech” (that copy has typos); the sheet’s “in his speech” is kept

speaker: Stage direction
quote: A rather cold woman
technique_notes: Foreshadows her moral callousness, rigid social snobbery, and total absence of maternal or civic empathy, establishing her immediately as an unyielding defender of class boundaries.
context: Opening stage direction introducing Sybil Birling.
note: describes Mrs Birling. Suggests she is cold-hearted and lacks compassion and empathy

speaker: Stage direction
quote: Her husband’s social superior
technique_notes: Establishes that Sybil comes from old, landed gentry, marrying down commercially while Arthur marries up socially. This imbalance keeps Arthur insecure and makes Sybil the strict domestic guardian of aristocratic decorum.
context: Opening stage direction defining Sybil Birling’s pedigree.
note: describes Mrs Birling. She comes from upper-class aristocracy but has had to marry a wealthy middle-class businessman

speaker: Stage direction
quote: Very pleased with life and rather excited
technique_notes: Highlights Sheila’s initial naivety, sheltered privilege, and self-centred domestic focus. Priestley establishes this baseline of shallow contentment so her subsequent moral awakening (anagnorisis) carries maximum dramatic force.
context: Opening stage direction during the engagement dinner.
note: describes Sheila Birling. It suggests that she is “pleased” with the sheltered, privileged life she leads, and is particularly excited by her engagement to Gerald

speaker: Stage direction
quote: Easy, well-bred young man-about-town
technique_notes: Captures Gerald’s effortless polish, charm, and elite confidence. The label “man-about-town” hints at moral carelessness, foreshadowing his casual exploitation of working-class women under the guise of gentlemanly gallantry.
context: Opening stage direction describing Gerald.
note: describes Gerald Croft. Highlights how he is a respected gentleman in the community who comes from a highly regarded upper-class family

speaker: Stage direction
quote: Not quite at ease, half shy, half assertive
technique_notes: Signals Eric’s deep internal conflict, alienation from his overbearing father, and underlying instability. The friction between “shy” and “assertive” hints at repressed guilt and an explosive lack of emotional self-control.
context: Opening stage direction describing Eric.
note: describes Eric Birling. Highlights how uncomfortable he seems, perhaps because he has a distant relationship with his family or perhaps because he is hiding a secret

speaker: Mr Birling
quote: We may look forward to the time when Crofts and Birlings are no longer competing but are working together – for lower costs and higher prices
note: Mr Birling treats the engagement like a business deal between his family and the Crofts

speaker: Mr Birling
quote: We hard-headed, practical businessmen
note: Mr Birling believes he is practical and sensible, but also shows he does not value sympathy or compassion for others. His only concern is making money, not helping society

speaker: Mr Birling
quote: Unsinkable, absolutely unsinkable
technique_notes: Priestley deliberately demolishes Birling’s credibility with the 1945 audience from the outset. Birling’s foolish belief in commercial and technological invulnerability directly mirrors his blindness to the impending catastrophe of two world wars.
Repetition – “unsinkable, absolutely unsinkable”: Birling’s repeated, emphatic boast shows his arrogant overconfidence in progress.
Dramatic irony – The 1945 audience knows the Titanic sank, so Birling’s certainty makes him look foolish and undermines his judgement.
context: Pontificating about industrial progress and the Titanic to Gerald and Eric.
note: Mr Birling believes that the Titanic will never sink, highlighting his arrogance and foolishness

speaker: Mr Birling
quote: Like bees in a hive – community and all that nonsense
technique_notes: Birling trivialises collective solidarity as chaotic, insect-like conformity. By branding social responsibility as “nonsense”, his unbridled individualism acts as the moral cue that summons the Inspector’s doorbell. (The sheet also lists “Cranks” with this quote.)
context: Dismissing socialist principles immediately before Goole arrives.
note: Mr Birling makes sarcastic comments about socialist ideas, showing how he is capitalist

speaker: Mr Birling
quote: A man has to mind his own business and look after himself and his own
note: Mr Birling lectures Gerald and Eric, revealing how he thinks people should be selfish

speaker: Mr Birling
quote: Well, it’s my duty to keep labour costs down
techniques: Subversion of the abstract noun “duty” / capitalist ideology.
technique_notes: Birling redefines moral “duty” as purely economic self-interest and profit preservation. In his world, civic and human obligations are entirely subordinated to balance sheets and shareholder margins.
context: Justifying refusing Eva Smith and her fellow strikers fair wages.
note: Mr Birling explaining to the Inspector why he refused to give Eva Smith fairer pay

speaker: Mr Birling
quote: If you don’t come down sharply on some of these people, they’d soon be asking for the earth
technique_notes: Birling presents a modest plea for twenty-five shillings a week as an existential rebellion. His punitive phrasing (“come down sharply”) treats working-class employees not as human collaborators, but as an unruly mass requiring constant suppression.
context: Defending his decision to discharge Eva Smith.
note: Mr Birling justifies why he fired Eva Smith, showing a lack of empathy towards her

speaker: Inspector Goole
quote: It’s better to ask for the earth than to take it
technique_notes: Goole contrasts the humble petitions of impoverished workers (“ask”) with the aggressive, entitled plunder of capitalist factory owners (“take”), framing capitalist accumulation as institutionalised theft.
context: Direct counter to Birling’s complaint about striking workers.
note: The Inspector’s quick response to Mr Birling. He challenges Mr Birling’s views, showing how Capitalists often selfishly “take” from others with no regard for the impact it has

speaker: Sheila
quote: Look – Mummy – isn’t it a beauty?
technique_notes: Illustrates Sheila’s opening state of infantilised dependence. Her excitement is tied directly to an expensive commodity, viewing affection through the lens of bourgeois consumerism.
context: Admiring her diamond engagement ring.
note: Sheila describing how beautiful her engagement ring is. Highlights how superficial and spoilt she is. Also, the way she says “Mummy” and “Daddy” highlights how childish and sheltered she is

speaker: Mr Birling
quote: Nothing to do with you, Sheila. Run along
technique_notes: Demonstrates the Edwardian patronisation of women, treating them as emotionally fragile ornaments to be shielded from public realities, while seeking to prevent younger family members from witnessing moral scrutiny.
context: Attempting to dismiss Sheila when the Inspector begins interrogating him.
note: Mr Birling tries to exclude Sheila from conversation with the Inspector. Perhaps shows how he regards women as emotionally fragile. Also, highlights how he treats her like a child

speaker: Sheila
quote: I can’t help thinking about this girl destroying herself – and I’ve been so happy tonight
note: Sheila feeling sorry for Eva. The two characters are foils (contrasting characters), both young women who have faced very different lives because of their social class

speaker: Sheila
quote: But these girls aren’t cheap labour – they’re people
technique_notes: Marks Sheila’s decisive moral shift. By replacing her father’s dehumanising economic label (“cheap labour”) with “people”, she strips away capitalist doublespeak to assert common human value.
context: Reacting to the news of Eva Smith’s dismissal from the factory.
note: Sheila challenges her father’s capitalist views. She humanises the working class and sees them as “people”. This contrasts to Mr Birling who sees them as “labour” to simply use and exploit

speaker: Inspector Goole
quote: So you used the power you had… to punish the girl?
note: The Inspector interrogates Sheila. Sheila abused her power to make sure Eva was fired from Milwards. She was jealous and angry that Eva suited a dress that did not look good on her

speaker: Sheila
quote: (laughs rather hysterically) Why – you fool – he knows. Of course he knows
technique_notes: Sheila sheds her submissive domestic role and echoes the Inspector’s incisive clarity. She recognises Goole not as an ordinary police officer, but as an omniscient moral force whom it is impossible to deceive.
context: Confronting Gerald at the end of Act 1 over Daisy Renton.
note: Sheila telling Gerald he is foolish if he thinks he can lie to the Inspector. She knows that it is better to be honest and to accept the guilt for what they have done

speaker: Stage direction
quote: Inspector Goole
technique_notes: “Goole” is an explicit homophone for “ghoul”, evoking a spirit or supernatural entity that feasts on the dead. This positions him beyond mortal policing: he acts as an uncanny, metaphysical harbinger, a manifestation of the collective guilt of the Birlings, or an emissary of divine judgment.
context: The name of the central inquisitor.
note: The Inspector’s name, “Goole” is a homophone for “ghoul”, meaning ghost. This could represent how he has supernatural powers or could be symbolic of God and the Holy Ghost

speaker: Stage direction
quote: Cutting in, massively
technique_notes: The Inspector asserts total narrative and physical control over the stage. “Cutting in” disrupts the patriarchal family hierarchy, while “massively” conveys an immovable, monolithic moral force that Birling’s civic status cannot intimidate or derail.
context: Repeated stage direction governing Goole’s interruptions of Birling.
note: stage direction describing how the Inspector interrupts the Birlings and Gerald while they speak. Emphasises how he is a strong, powerful force that cannot be overcome

speaker: Stage direction
quote: He speaks carefully, weightily
technique_notes: Contrasts sharply with Birling’s excitable, arrogant rambling. Goole’s deliberate, measured delivery establishes intellectual and moral command; every phrase carries philosophical weight and judicial gravity.
context: Opening stage direction introducing the Inspector’s manner of speech.
note: stage directions describing how the Inspector speaks. He speaks carefully because he is in control of both his words and the situation. Also, his words carry much power and importance

speaker: Inspector Goole
quote: A chain of events
technique_notes: Introduces Priestley’s core disciplinary concept of causality. Each individual cruelty acts as an interlocking link, demonstrating that moral accountability is cumulative and that seemingly minor acts of selfishness produce devastating collective consequences.
context: Goole explaining how individual actions contributed to Eva’s suicide.
note: The Inspector describes how not one factor, but numerous factors, all contributed to Eva’s death. This highlights how each of them are responsible

speaker: Stage direction
quote: Eva Smith
technique_notes: “Eva” recalls Eve (the biblical mother of all living humanity), while “Smith” is the most common British working-class surname, transforming her into an Everyman figure for the labouring masses. “Daisy” evokes a common, easily crushed field flower, while “Renton” hints at the financial desperation that forced her to rent out her body to survive.
context: The two names used by the victim across the narrative.
note: Eva’s name is significant. The surname “Smith” is a common, working-class surname, suggesting she represents the working class. “Eva” is a variation of “Eve”, the first woman created by God in the Bible, suggesting she represents the experiences of working-class women

speaker: Inspector Goole
quote: She’d swallowed a lot of strong disinfectant. Burnt her inside out
techniques: Visceral sensory imagery / graphic physical description.
technique_notes: The grotesque, physical detail of being “burnt inside out” shatters the polite, sanitised atmosphere of the dining room. Disinfectant cleanses surface dirt; Eva using it internally acts as a horrific metaphor for a desperate, corrupted society destroying itself from within.
context: The Inspector bluntly describing Eva Smith’s suicide to the family in Act 1.
note: The Inspector describing how Eva Smith died. It was a very violent and gruesome suicide

speaker: Inspector Goole
quote: No relatives to help her, few friends, lonely, half-starved, she was feeling desperate
technique_notes: The cumulative list of privations highlights the absolute absence of a social safety net in 1912 Edwardian Britain. “Half-starved” sharply contrasts with the Birlings’ lavish port and dinner party, exposing the lethal consequences of capitalist abandonment.
context: Goole recounting Eva’s period of unemployment after Birling fired her.
note: The Inspector describing Eva when she was unemployed for two months after Mr Birling fired her from the factory. “Half-starved” shows how impoverished she is, contrasting to the Birlings who are enjoying fine dining to celebrate Sheila and Gerald’s engagement

speaker: Inspector Goole
quote: It would do us all a bit of good if we put ourselves in the place of these young women counting their pennies in their dingy little back bedrooms
techniques: Visual imagery / didactic appeal for radical empathy.
technique_notes: Goole explicitly models socialist empathy. Juxtaposing the minute domestic reality of “counting their pennies” in “dingy little back bedrooms” against Birling’s expansive wealth demands that the bourgeois elite look beyond abstract economic figures to acknowledge the claustrophobic lived reality of the working class.
context: Goole rebuking Birling’s lack of sympathy for his female factory staff.
note: The Inspector speaking to the Birlings. He suggests that it is important to show empathy to those who are less fortunate in society. The play says “if sometimes we tried to put ourselves in the place of…”; the sheet shortens it

speaker: Inspector Goole
quote: Public men, Mr Birling, have responsibilities as well as privileges
technique_notes: Directly challenges the Edwardian social contract, asserting that civic honours, power, and wealth demand equal moral accountability to the public good.
context: Interrupting Birling’s attempts to invoke his civic status.
note: Only on the mid-point sheet

speaker: Inspector Goole
quote: We are members of one body
technique_notes: Priestley appropriates Christian scripture to validate democratic socialism. Society is framed as an interdependent physical organism: harm inflicted on the most vulnerable part inevitably poisons and destroys the collective whole.
Metaphor – “members of one body”: Society is shown as a single body, so harming one part harms the whole.
Allusion – Echoes the Christian idea of the body of Christ: Priestley uses Biblical authority to support social responsibility.
context: The theological and political climax of Goole’s farewell sermon.
note: Only on the mid-point sheet

speaker: Mrs Birling
quote: You seem to have made a great impression on this child, Inspector.
technique_notes: Foils – Sheila’s guilt is set against Mr Birling’s lack of guilt, so her moral growth stands out and the older generation looks stubborn.
Juxtaposition – Mrs Birling’s patronising “child” is opposed by the Inspector’s view that being “impressionable” is a moral virtue: the two generations’ values clash.
Adjective – “great”: shows how much Sheila has changed; she has made a real impact on the Inspector.

Mrs Birling uses the noun “child” to infantilise Sheila, attempting to dismiss her moral awakening as mere youthful fragility and keep her silenced within the domestic sphere. Inspector Goole subverts this condescension by reframing being “impressionable” as a vital moral virtue rather than a weakness. In the 1912 setting, Edwardian society demanded total obedience to patriarchal authority; for Priestley’s 1945 audience, Sheila’s generation was the one that lived through two catastrophic world wars caused by the hubris and complacency of men like Arthur Birling, and stood at the ballot box in 1945 to vote in a Labour government and establish the welfare state.
context: Early Act 2, when Mrs Birling enters the dining room and attempts to patronise Sheila’s emotional distress and growing sense of guilt.
note: Only on the mid-point sheet (first half of its quote 28)

speaker: Inspector Goole
quote: We often do on the young ones. They’re more impressionable.
techniques: Generational antithesis / patronising epithet vs moral validation.
technique_notes: Mrs Birling uses the noun “child” to infantilise Sheila, attempting to dismiss her moral awakening as mere youthful fragility and keep her silenced within the domestic sphere. Inspector Goole subverts this condescension by reframing being “impressionable” as a vital moral virtue rather than a weakness. In the 1912 setting, Edwardian society demanded total obedience to patriarchal authority; for Priestley’s 1945 audience, Sheila’s generation was the one that lived through two catastrophic world wars caused by the hubris and complacency of men like Arthur Birling, and stood at the ballot box in 1945 to vote in a Labour government and establish the welfare state.
context: Early Act 2, when Mrs Birling enters the dining room and attempts to patronise Sheila’s emotional distress and growing sense of guilt.
note: Only on the mid-point sheet (second half of its quote 28)

speaker: Inspector Goole
quote: Daisy Renton
technique_notes: “Eva” recalls Eve (the biblical mother of all living humanity), while “Smith” is the most common British working-class surname, transforming her into an Everyman figure for the labouring masses. “Daisy” evokes a common, easily crushed field flower, while “Renton” hints at the financial desperation that forced her to rent out her body to survive.
context: The two names used by the victim across the narrative.
note: Only on the mid-point sheet (the second name of the victim, part of its quote 17)

speaker: Sheila
quote: If I could help her now – I would!
note: From Lesson 10 (young vs older generations): Sheila’s reaction, contrasted with Mr Birling’s “asking for the earth” line.

speaker: Sheila
quote: (with sharp sarcasm) You were the wonderful fairy prince
note: From Lessons 11 and 14: Sheila to Gerald about his affair with Daisy Renton.

speaker: Mrs Birling
quote: As if a girl of that sort would refuse money!
note: From Lesson 13: Mrs Birling on Eva’s refusal of the charity’s help. The play has “would ever refuse money”; the lesson omits “ever”.

speaker: Inspector Goole
quote: You used her… as if she was an animal, a thing, not a person
note: From Lesson 14: the Inspector to Eric. The play has “Just used her for the end of a stupid drunken evening, as if she was an animal, a thing, not a person.”

speaker: Eric
quote: You killed her – and the child she’d have had too – my child
note: From Lesson 14: Eric to Mrs Birling.

speaker: Inspector Goole
quote: One Eva Smith has gone but there are millions and millions and millions still left with us
note: From Lesson 15: the Inspector’s final speech. The play continues “of Eva Smiths and John Smiths still left with us”; the lesson shortens it.

speaker: Inspector Goole
quote: If men will not learn that lesson, they will be taught it in fire and blood and anguish
technique_notes: Imagery – “fire and blood and anguish”: Violent, painful images of war warn of the suffering that will follow if people ignore the lesson.
Metaphor – “taught it in fire and blood”: Learning is presented as punishment, with war as the teacher.
Dramatic irony – The 1945 audience has lived through two world wars, so they know the warning came true.
Audience – Written for people who had just experienced war, so the Inspector’s warning feels urgent and aimed at them.
note: From Lesson 15: the Inspector’s final speech. The play has “then they will be taught it in fire and blood and anguish”.

speaker: Inspector Goole
quote: You’ll be able to divide the responsibility between you when I’ve gone
note: From Lesson 16 (accountability).

speaker: Sheila
quote: I know I’m to blame – and I’m desperately sorry
note: From Lesson 14 quote quiz. In the play it continues “– but I can’t believe – I won’t believe – it’s simply my fault”.

speaker: Inspector Goole
quote: A girl died tonight… Died in misery and agony – hating life
note: From Lesson 14 quote quiz. The play has “A girl died tonight. A pretty, lively sort of girl… But she died in misery and agony – hating life”.

speaker: Stage direction
quote: Impression of massiveness, solidity, and purposefulness
note: From Lesson 14 quote quiz: the stage direction describing the Inspector.

quote: I met a traveller from an antique land
technique_notes: Guide labels: adjective “antique”; the speaker does not see the statue, he only hears about it from the traveller.

quote: My name is Ozymandias, King of Kings
technique_notes: “King of Kings” emphasises superiority and dominance, reflecting extreme pride and hubris.
note: Shows the ruler’s arrogance and belief in his absolute power.

quote: Look on my Works, ye Mighty, and despair!
technique_notes: the commanding verb “Look” asserts authority, but it is ironic because nothing of his power remains.
Imperative – “Look”: The command shows the king’s arrogant authority, demanding attention and awe.
Irony – The “Mighty” are told to despair at his works, but only ruins remain: his power is gone.
note: Shows how Ozymandias wanted others to fear and admire his power.

quote: Nothing beside remains
technique_notes: the abruptness highlights emptiness, contrasting with his earlier arrogance.
note: Reveals that all of Ozymandias’ power and achievements have disappeared over time.

quote: The lone and level sands stretch far away
technique_notes: “lone and level” creates a sense of endless emptiness, emphasising how nature outlasts human ambition.
Imagery – “lone and level sands stretch far away”: Vast, empty desert imagery shows nothing is left of the king’s empire.
Alliteration – “lone and level”: The repeated “l” sound creates a flat, drawn-out effect that echoes the endless emptiness.
note: Shows the vast, timeless power of nature compared to human power.

quote: Round the decay of that colossal wreck
technique_notes: Guide label: juxtaposition of what the statue says with “decay” and “wreck”.

quote: Sneer of cold command
technique_notes: Lesson labels: the adjective “cold”; alliteration of “c”.

quote: Chartered streets
technique_notes: Guide labels (“chartered streets” and “chartered Thames”): adjective “chartered”; repetition; symbol of the river Thames.
note: The anthology spells it “chartered” (the poem’s original has “charter’d”).

quote: Mind-forg’d manacles
technique_notes: “manacles” suggests imprisonment, while “mind-forg’d” implies people are trapped by their own thoughts or by society’s ideas, highlighting psychological oppression.
note: Shows how people are mentally trapped and controlled by society. The anthology spells it “mind-forged” (the original has “mind-forg’d”).

quote: Runs in blood down palace walls
technique_notes: “blood” represents violence and sacrifice, while “palace walls” symbolise the monarchy, implying their power is built on the suffering of others.
Imagery – “blood” down “palace walls”: A vivid picture of violence staining the seat of power.
Symbol – “blood” represents violence and sacrifice; “palace walls” symbolise the monarchy, whose power is built on others’ suffering.
note: Suggests that the ruling classes are responsible for the suffering and deaths of ordinary people.

quote: Blackning Church appalls
technique_notes: “blackning” suggests moral corruption, while the Church symbolises institutions that should protect people but instead contribute to their suffering.
note: Critiques the Church for being corrupt and failing to help the poor.

quote: Youthful Harlots
technique_notes: Guide label: symbol of “harlots”.

quote: Small circles glittering idly
technique_notes: the ripples symbolise the way human actions disturb the natural world, while the repeated “s” sound creates a snake-like effect, suggesting temptation and foreshadowing his downfall.
Symbol – The “small circles” (ripples) symbolise the way human actions disturb the natural world.
Sibilance – The repeated “s” sounds create a snake-like effect, suggesting temptation and foreshadowing his downfall.
note: Shows the speaker’s arrogance at the start of the poem, as he disturbs the stillness of nature without thinking about the consequences.

quote: The grim shape towered up between me and the stars
technique_notes: the mountain is given a threatening presence through “towered,” while “grim shape” suggests fear and the unknown, emphasising the sublime power of nature.
Imagery – “grim shape towered”: A dark, looming image makes the mountain frightening and shows the power of nature.
Personification – The mountain “towered” as if it were chasing him, giving it a threatening presence.
note: Shows the overwhelming and frightening power of nature as the mountain rises above the speaker and makes him feel small and powerless.

quote: Huge and mighty forms… were a trouble to my dreams
technique_notes: “huge” and “mighty” emphasise nature’s omnipotence, while “trouble to my dreams” shows that the encounter continues to disturb him psychologically.
note: Shows that the experience has permanently changed the speaker, leaving him haunted and humbled by the power of nature.

quote: My Last Duchess
technique_notes: Guide/lesson labels: possessive pronoun “my” (ownership); adjective “last”; the title “Duchess”; the Duchess is never given a name or voice.

quote: That’s my last Duchess painted on the wall
technique_notes: “my” suggests ownership and control, while “Duchess” reduces her to her status rather than her identity, showing how she is objectified and disempowered.
note: Shows how the Duke sees the Duchess as his possession rather than an independent person.

quote: I gave commands; then all smiles stopped together
technique_notes: the vague phrase “gave commands” hides the brutality of his actions, while the pause emphasises the finality of her death.
Euphemism – “gave commands”: A vague phrase that hides the brutality of what the Duke actually ordered.
Caesura – The pause before “all smiles stopped” emphasises the finality of her death.
note: Implied that the Duke had the Duchess killed because he was jealous and controlling.

quote: Notice Neptune, though, taming a sea-horse
technique_notes: Neptune symbolises male power and domination, reflecting how the Duke sees himself as someone who should control others; the imperative “Notice” also reveals his arrogance and need to direct attention.
Symbol – Neptune taming a sea-horse symbolises male power and domination, the way the Duke sees himself.
Imperative – “Notice”: Shows his arrogance and his need to direct the listener’s attention.
note: Shows the Duke’s obsession with control and power.

poem: The Charge of the Light Brigade
quote: Into the mouth of Hell
technique_notes: compares the battlefield to “hell,” suggesting horror and sacrifice. The metaphor glorifies the soldiers’ courage while also showing the destructiveness and futility of war.
Metaphor – The battlefield is “the mouth of Hell”, suggesting horror and the destructiveness of war.
Symbol – “Hell” represents the suffering and futility of war, though the soldiers’ courage is also glorified.
note: Shows the soldiers’ bravery as they charge into almost certain death.

poem: The Charge of the Light Brigade
quote: Honour the Light Brigade, noble six hundred
technique_notes: “Honour” and “noble” idealise the soldiers, reflecting patriotic pride and the way society glorifies sacrifice while ignoring the tragedy behind it.
note: Encourages readers to celebrate the soldiers’ bravery despite their pointless deaths.

poem: The Charge of the Light Brigade
quote: Someone had blundered
technique_notes: Lesson labels: “someone” (those in command mentioned in passing) is juxtaposed with the repeated “noble six hundred”; the verb “blundered”.
note: The anthology has “Some one had blunder’d”.

quote: Our brains ache
technique_notes: “our” suggests unity and shared pain among soldiers, while “ache” captures the dull persistence of suffering from cold and fear.
Verb – “ache”: Captures the dull, persistent suffering from cold and fear.
Pronoun – “our”: Suggests unity and shared pain among the soldiers.
note: Shows shared exhaustion and suffering in harsh war conditions.

quote: The merciless iced east winds that knive us
technique_notes: the wind is given human cruelty through “knive,” suggesting deliberate violence. Nature becomes a more relentless attacker than the soldiers’ human foes.
note: Presents nature as the soldiers’ true enemy.

quote: All their eyes are ice
technique_notes: Lesson labels (“Half-known faces. All their eyes are ice”): third-person pronoun “their”; symbol “eyes”; adjective “half-known”; metaphor “eyes are ice” (ice is brittle and fragile).
Metaphor – “eyes are ice”: Ice is brittle and fragile, suggesting the soldiers are frozen, numb and close to death.
Symbol – “eyes”: Represent the men’s inner lives, which are frozen and emptied by the war.

quote: We are prepared: we build our houses squat
Spits like a tame cat turned savage
technique_notes: Guide labels: simile; juxtaposition of “tame” and “savage”.
Simile – “like a tame cat turned savage”: The sea, usually familiar and calm, suddenly turns wild and dangerous.
Juxtaposition – “tame” against “savage”: The contrast shows how quickly nature can turn from safe to threatening.

quote: Blows full blast
technique_notes: Guide labels: plosive consonants create the sound of the storm; the semantic field of war (e.g. “blast”).

quote: Bombarded by the empty air
technique_notes: Guide labels: violent verb “bombarded”; symbolism of the “empty air”.

quote: King, honour, human dignity, etcetera
technique_notes: placing grand ideals next to “etcetera” trivialises them, showing how war reduces noble motives to empty words.
note: Mockingly lists patriotic values as meaningless in the panic of battle.

quote: Suddenly he awoke and was running
technique_notes: “Suddenly” and “running” create a sense of shock and chaos, reflecting how instinct takes over from reason during battle.
Verb – “running”: Shows instinct taking over in a sudden, frantic action.
Adverb – “Suddenly”: Creates a sense of shock and chaos.
note: Shows the soldier’s panic and instinctive reaction.

quote: His terror’s touchy dynamite
technique_notes: the metaphor of “dynamite” turns the soldier into something unstable and deadly, while “touchy” suggests fragility and the uncontrollable power of fear.
note: Shows how fear turns the soldier into a weapon, ready to explode with violence.

quote: A yellow hare that rolled like a flame
technique_notes: Lesson labels: hellish imagery “flame”; violent imagery (a dying rabbit); symbolism of the “hare”.

quote: His blood shadow
technique_notes: “blood” symbolises guilt and violence, while “shadow” suggests an inescapable reminder of his actions that haunts him psychologically.
Metaphor – “blood shadow”: The shadow is a metaphor for guilt that follows him everywhere.
Symbol – “blood” symbolises guilt and violence; “shadow” is an inescapable reminder that haunts him.
note: Shows how guilt and trauma follow the soldier after the killing.

quote: Probably armed, possibly not
technique_notes: the contrast between “probably” and “possibly” captures the soldier’s doubt and the mental conflict that remains long after the event.
note: Highlights uncertainty and guilt about whether the killing was justified.

quote: Tosses his guts back into his body
technique_notes: “tosses” sounds casual and careless, showing how desensitised soldiers become; the graphic image reinforces the horror of war.
Imagery – “guts”: A graphic, shocking image that reinforces the horror of war.
Colloquial language – “tosses”: A casual, careless tone shows how desensitised soldiers have become.
note: Brutally describes the soldier cleaning up after the shooting.

quote: But I blink and he bursts again
technique_notes: Lesson labels: symbolism (when he closes his eyes he remembers the soldier); enjambment; plosive “b”; violent verb “bursts”.

quote: End of story, except not really
technique_notes: Lesson: this is the volta; the conflict has moved from the battlefield to the soldier’s mind, and the poem focuses on the aftermath of war.

quote: On another occasion
technique_notes: Lesson: the poem starts in the middle of the action, suggesting this story is one of many that haunt the soldier.

quote: Spasms of paper red
technique_notes: “spasms” implies both grief and violence, linking remembrance with physical pain and the bloodshed of war.
note: Suggests both the delicate nature of the poppy and the pain of loss.

quote: The gelled blackthorns of your hair
technique_notes: “blackthorns” recall Christ’s crown of thorns, symbolising suffering and sacrifice; “gelled” creates a tender, realistic image of her son.
note: Shows both love and pain; motherhood mixed with sacrifice.

quote: Running children in a nightmare heat
technique_notes: “nightmare heat” evokes terror and pain; the children symbolise innocence destroyed by violence and humanity’s indifference to suffering.
Imagery – “nightmare heat”: Evokes terror and pain.
Symbol – The “running children” symbolise innocence destroyed by violence.
note: Refers to victims of war, showing the suffering caused by human conflict.

quote: In his darkroom he is finally alone
technique_notes: the “darkroom” represents both his professional space and his internal world (inside his mind), where he must confront the moral weight of his photographs – his memories.
Juxtaposition – The quiet, private darkroom is set against the violence he has photographed, so he must face the moral weight of what he has seen.
Symbol – The “darkroom” represents both his professional space and his inner mind, where he confronts his memories.
note: Shows his isolation and emotional distance from both his work and others.

quote: Spools of suffering set out in ordered rows
technique_notes: “spools of suffering” compares the photographs to containers of human pain; their careful arrangement shows his attempt to impose control over trauma.
note: Highlights the contrast between the chaos of war and the order of his work.

quote: Belfast. Beirut. Phnom Penh.
technique_notes: Lesson labels: caesura; plosive consonants “b” and “p”; a list of three places of conflict.

quote: He earns his living and they do not care
technique_notes: Lesson labels: declarative statement (matter-of-fact tone); the final line of the poem; collective pronoun “they”.

quote: Paper kites
Let the daylight break through capitals and monoliths
technique_notes: Lesson: the semantic field of light (“luminous”, “daylight”) against the semantic field of hard stone (“buildings”, “capitals”, “monoliths”).

quote: Pages smoothed and stroked and turned transparent with attention
There was once a country… I left it as a child
technique_notes: Guide labels: the past tense “There was once”; the caesura.
note: The anthology has “There once was a country…”; the revision guide has “There was once a country…”.

quote: It may be sick with tyrants, but I am branded by an impression of sunlight
technique_notes: contrasts “tyrants” with “sunlight,” suggesting memory is powerful and idealised; “branded” implies the memory is permanent.
Metaphor – “branded by an impression of sunlight”: The memory is burned into her, permanent.
Juxtaposition – “tyrants” against “sunlight”: Contrasts the country’s cruelty with her idealised, warm memory of it.
note: Shows the speaker’s refusal to see her homeland negatively despite its political corruption.

quote: My shadow falls as evidence of sunlight
technique_notes: “shadow” represents her presence and identity, while “sunlight” symbolises hope and positive memory; suggests that even in exile, her past continues to define her.
Metaphor – “my shadow falls as evidence of sunlight”: Her shadow is proof of the light, so even in exile her past defines her.
Symbol – “shadow” represents her presence and identity; “sunlight” symbolises hope and positive memory.
note: Shows how the speaker’s identity is shaped by her memories of her homeland.

quote: It lies in front of me, docile as paper / I comb its hair and love its shining eyes
note: The anthology has “It lies down in front of me, docile as paper; / I comb its hair and love its shining eyes.”

quote: Bandage up me eye
technique_notes: Guide labels: the metaphor of being blinded; the Creole dialect “me”.

quote: Dem tell me
technique_notes: Guide labels: the pronoun “dem”; repetition (“Dem tell me / Dem tell me”).

quote: I carving out me identity
technique_notes: Guide label: the metaphor of “carving”.

quote: Toussaint de thorn
technique_notes: Lesson slide: “What does this symbol suggest?”

quote: A healing star… a yellow sunrise
technique_notes: Lesson slide: “What does this symbol suggest?” (about Mary Seacole).

quote: Head full of powerful incantations
technique_notes: “incantations” compares nationalistic ideas to spells, showing how the pilot’s thoughts are controlled by duty and expectation.
note: Suggests the pilot is brainwashed by patriotic propaganda.

quote: Fishes flashing silver
technique_notes: the image of “silver” symbolises purity and hope; the fish reflect the freedom and vitality of life, contrasting with his deathly mission.
note: Represents the beauty of life that tempts the pilot to turn back.

quote: Which had been the better way to die
technique_notes: contrasts physical death with social death, criticising the cruelty of cultural shame and misplaced ideas of honour.
Juxtaposition – Physical death is set against social death, criticising the cruelty of cultural shame.
Rhetorical question – “Which had been the better way to die”: Makes the reader weigh the two kinds of death and question misplaced ideas of honour.
note: Shows how society’s rejection of the pilot is worse than dying in battle.

speaker: Title
quote: The Modern Prometheus
context: Subtitle on the title page | Frankenstein lesson 1.
note: The alternative title of the novel. Shelley compares Victor to the myth of Prometheus

speaker: Walton
quote: His limbs were nearly frozen
note: Walton’s description of Victor when he pulls him onto the ship

speaker: Walton
quote: His body dreadfully emaciated
note: Walton’s description of Victor when he pulls him onto the ship

speaker: Walton
quote: His eyes have generally an expression of wildness, even madness
context: Novel: "wildness, and even madness" | Frankenstein lessons 3 and 7: windows to the soul; Victor’s mind is broken.
note: Walton’s description of Victor when he pulls him onto the ship

speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quote: My mother’s tender caresses and my father’s smile
note: Victor Frankenstein describes how his parents loved and cared for him

speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quote: I was their plaything and their idol
context: Frankenstein lesson 4: asked of the class.
note: Victor describes how his parents gave him a privileged and joyful childhood

speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quote: Life and death appeared to me ideal bounds, which I should first break through
note: Victor describing his desire to create life and transgress the laws of nature and religion

speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quote: A new species would bless me as its creator and source
note: Victor hopes to create a new species of creatures that will recognise him as their God

speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quote: I pursued nature to her hiding places
context: Frankenstein lesson 5: nature is presented as prey to be hunted; Victor hunts down nature’s secrets.
note: Victor describing how he seeks to transgress the laws of nature

speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quote: I shunned my fellow creatures as if I had been guilty of a crime
note: Victor describing how isolated he became during the creation of the creature

speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quote: Painful labour
context: Frankenstein lesson 7: childbirth imagery for the Creature’s birth.
note: Victor describing the hard work behind his creation of the creature

speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quote: The beauty of the dream vanished and breathless horror and disgust filled my heart
context: Frankenstein lesson 7: Victor’s horror and disgust.
note: Victor describing how he is immediately disgusted by the creature and rejects it

speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quote: Did I not as his maker owe him all the happiness that was in my power to bestow?
context: Novel: "all the portion of happiness that it was in my power to bestow"
note: Victor agrees to make a female creature because he believes it’s his duty as his creator

speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quote: I was a slave to my creature
context: Novel: "the slave of my creature" (teacher: "a slave to my creature")
note: Victor feels like he is controlled by the creature and must obey him

speaker: The Creature
quote: You are my creator, but I am your master. Obey!
note: The Creature demands Victor to make him a female creature and tells him to obey

speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quote: No creature had ever been so miserable as I
note: Victor believes he is the most miserable living creature in existence

speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quote: One by one, my friends were snatched away; I was left desolate
note: Victor describes how his loved ones have all been taken by the Creature, leaving him alone

speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quote: The death of William, the execution of Justine, the murder of Clerval, and lastly of my wife
note: Victor lists all the victims of the Creature

speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quote: I was the true murderer
context: Novel: "I, not in deed, but in effect, was the true murderer" (also "But I, the true murderer" earlier in Chapter 8)
note: Victor feels like he is truly responsible for the death of William and Justine

speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quote: I bore a hell within me which nothing could extinguish
note: Victor describing how the guilt he feels for the deaths of William and Justine is unbearable and will never go

speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quote: Like the archangel who aspired to omnipotence, I am chained in an eternal hell
note: Victor describes how he aspired for power but it led to his downfall

speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quote: Demoniacal corpse
context: Frankenstein lesson 7: nightmarish imagery.
note: Victor describing the Creature, on the night he creates him

speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quote: Begone! Vile insect!
technique_notes: Metaphor – “vile insect”: The Creature is compared to an insect, showing Victor sees him as disgusting and beneath him.
Imperative – “Begone!”: A harsh command that shows Victor’s rejection and fear.
context: Frankenstein lesson 15: Victor holds the power and dehumanises the Creature.
note: Victor rejects the Creature when they meet on the mountain

speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quote: Monster
context: Victor uses "monster" many times; first in Chapter 5
note: Victor describing the Creature. The Creature later calls himself this too

speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quote: Fiend
context: "fiend" is used many times (e.g. Chapters 9, 16, 20)
note: Victor describing the Creature. The Creature later calls himself this too

speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quote: Demon
context: 1818 text spells it "dæmon" (e.g. Chapter 7); used many times
note: Victor describes the Creature

speaker: William
quote: Ogre
context: William says "ogre" in Chapter 16
note: William describing the Creature

speaker: Felix and Agatha
quote: Good spirit
context: Novel: "good spirit, wonderful" (the cottagers' words; Creature overhears)
note: Felix and Agatha believe that the Creature is a spirit helping their family

speaker: The Creature
quote: I was benevolent and good; misery made me a fiend
note: The Creature explains that he was once good, but his painful experiences have made him a monster

speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quote: One hand was stretched out, seemingly to detain me
note: Victor describing the Creature reaching out to him. He thinks it is trying to attack him

speaker: The Creature
quote: Barbarous villagers
note: The Creature describing the villagers who attacked him

speaker: The Creature
quote: The barbarity of man
note: The Creature describing the villagers who attacked him

speaker: The Creature
quote: Low hovel
note: The Creature describing the hovel that becomes his home

speaker: The Creature
quote: My kennel
note: The Creature describing the hovel that becomes his home

speaker: The Creature
quote: Carpeted with straw
context: Novel: "carpeted it with clean straw"
note: The Creature describing the hovel that becomes his home

speaker: The Creature
quote: Who was I? What was I? Whence did I come?
note: The Creature questions who and what he is

speaker: The Creature
quote: Was I a monster, a blot upon the earth?
context: Novel: "Was I, then, a monster, a blot upon the earth"
note: He believes that he must simply be a monster, because this is how he is treated by others

speaker: The Creature
quote: No father had watched my infant days; no mother had blessed me with smiles
note: The Creature explains that he was deprived of loving parents and a family

speaker: The Creature
quote: I ought to be thy Adam, but I am rather the fallen angel
technique_notes: Metaphor – “the fallen angel”: The Creature compares himself to Satan cast out of Heaven: once good, now abandoned.
Religious imagery – Adam and the fallen angel: Links to Paradise Lost; Victor, like God, abandoned his creation.
context: Frankenstein lesson 15: the Creature compares himself to Satan.
note: When he meets him on the mountain, the Creature tells Victor that he should treat him like Adam, but he has become the devil

speaker: The Creature
quote: Broken the only link that held me to the world
note: The Creature explains that when the De Laceys rejected him, this was a turning point

speaker: The Creature
quote: Forced solitude
note: The Creature explains how he was completely rejected by the whole of society

speaker: The Creature
quote: Shall each man find a wife, and each beast have his mate, and I be alone?
context: Novel: "Shall each man, find a wife for his bosom, and each beast have his mate, and I be alone?"
note: The Creature asks Victor why he should be the only living creature to be alone

speaker: The Creature
quote: The love of another will destroy the cause of my crimes
note: The Creature explains to Victor that if he has a female companion to show him love and kindness, he will no longer be a cruel monster

speaker: The Creature
quote: I, like the arch-fiend, bore a hell within me
technique_notes: Metaphor – “a hell within me”: His inner torment and guilt are compared to Hell.
Allusion – “arch-fiend”: Refers to Satan in Milton’s Paradise Lost, linking the Creature to the fallen angel.
context: Frankenstein lessons 15-17: links to Satan’s “Myself am Hell”.
note: The Creature describes how the rage and hatred turns him into a monster and a devil

speaker: The Creature
quote: My heart swelled with hellish triumph
context: Novel: "my heart swelled with exultation and hellish triumph" | Frankenstein lesson 17.
note: The Creature feels a sense of power when murdering William

speaker: The Creature
quote: I too can create desolation
context: Frankenstein lesson 17: “too” suggests he realises he is like others.
note: The Creature feels a sense of power when murdering William

speaker: The Creature
quote: Beware, for I am fearless and therefore powerful
note: The Creature tells Victor that he is powerful because he has nothing to lose or fear

speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quote: I was the slave, not the master, of an impulse which I detested yet could not disobey
context: Sheet says The Creature, but in the novel it is Victor speaking (about his urge for revenge), so speaker changed to Victor Frankenstein
note: The Creature tells Walton that he was controlled by his rage and hatred

speaker: The Creature
quote: Polluted by crimes and torn by the bitterest remorse, where can I find rest but in death?
note: The Creature tells Walton how he feels internally broken and only death will bring him peace

speaker: Walton
quote: Undiscovered solitudes
note: Robert Walton describing the undiscovered and isolated place he travels to

speaker: Walton
quote: Dear Margaret, do I not deserve to accomplish some great purpose?
note: Walton suggesting that he is destined for greatness and feels entitled to success

speaker: Walton
quote: I bitterly feel the want of a friend
note: Walton describing how lonely and isolated he feels on his voyage

speaker: Walton
quote: The brother of my heart
note: Walton describing his deep friendship and connection with Victor

speaker: Walton
quote: One man’s life or death were but a small price to pay for the knowledge which I sought
context: Novel: "for the acquirement of the knowledge which I sought" (teacher: "for the knowledge which I sought")
note: Walton describing how he is determined to succeed, but this also shows how reckless he is

speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quote: Whither does your senseless curiosity lead you?
note: When Walton asks for details about the creation of the Creature, Victor tells him how foolish he is for wanting to go down the path that he went. Shelley suggests that Walton perhaps has not truly learnt from Victor’s example. However, he does turn his ship back home

speaker: The Creature
quote: I longed to join them, but I dared not
context: Creature watching the De Lacey family; check wording against the teacher sheet (not found word-for-word)
note: The Creature describes how he desperately wants to be part of their family, but fears that they will reject him, like the others who have attacked or rejected him

speaker: The Creature
quote: Who can describe their horror and consternation on beholding me?
note: The creature describes the shock and disgust the De Laceys feel when they see him

speaker: Elizabeth
quote: Sweet laughing blue eyes
context: Frankenstein lesson 7: William’s eyes show innocence.
note: In a letter to Victor, Elizabeth describes William’s bright blue eyes

speaker: The Creature
quote: This little creature was unprejudiced
note: The Creature sees William and believes he will be kind to him because he’s an innocent child

speaker: William
quote: You are an ogre
note: William immediately sees the Creature as a monster and treats him cruelly

speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quote: The saintly sufferer
note: Victor describing Justine Moritz as a pure and innocent victim

speaker: The Creature
quote: It stirred the fiend within me – not I, but she, shall suffer
note: The Creature assumes Justine will be cruel to him, so decides to make her suffer

speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quote: The judges had already condemned my unhappy victim
note: Victor describes how Justine was assumed guilty and not given a fair trial

speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quote: The tortures of the accused did not equal mine
note: Victor describes how he is suffering inside even more than Justine

speaker: Justine
quote: I began to think that I was the monster he said I was
context: Novel: "I almost began to think that I was the monster that he said I was" (the confessor, not the interrogator, says it)
note: Justine describing how, after being told she was a monster by the interrogator and so many people, she began to believe she was

speaker: Elizabeth
quote: Men appear to me as monsters thirsting for each other’s blood
context: Frankenstein lesson 9: said after Justine’s execution; shows Elizabeth’s realisation that society is cruel.
note: Elizabeth describes how, after Justine’s trial and execution, she considers society to be the true monster

speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quote: The image of Clerval was forever before me, ghastly and murdered
note: Victor is haunted by the image of seeing Clerval’s dead body

speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quote: My friend and dearest companion had fallen victim to me and the monster of my creation
context: Novel: "Clerval, my friend and dearest companion, had fallen a victim to me and the monster of my creation"
note: Victor believes that he is responsible for the murder of Clerval

speaker: Victor’s mother
quote: Pretty present
context: Frankenstein lesson 4: treats Elizabeth as an object.
note: Victor’s mother describes Elizabeth as a present for Victor

speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quote: Promised gift
note: Victor describes Elizabeth as his gift

speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quote: Till death she was to be mine only
note: Victor falls in love with Elizabeth and he decides that they will be together forever

speaker: The Creature
quote: I shall be with you on your wedding night
context: Appears more than once in the novel; chapter shown is the first.
note: The Creature promises to get revenge on Victor on his wedding night

speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quote: He seemed to jeer, as with his fiendish finger he pointed towards the corpse of my wife
note: Victor describes the Creature laughing at the dead body of Elizabeth

speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quote: My heart often sickened at the work of my hands
note: Victor describes making the female companion and is disgusted by his work

speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quote: A race of devils would be propagated upon the earth
note: Victor worries that the two monsters will have children that will spread across the world

speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quote: The wickedness of my promise burst upon me
note: Victor suddenly changes his mind and believes it is a mistake to make another creature

speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quote: A ghastly grin wrinkled his lips
note: Victor describes seeing the Creature’s smiling face watching his work through the window

speaker: Victor Frankenstein
quote: Inarticulate sounds
context: Appears more than once in the novel; chapter shown is the first. | Frankenstein lesson 7: childbirth imagery for the Creature’s birth.
note: The Creature tries to speak to Victor when he is born, but he just makes noises like a baby (on the midpoint list only)
